mainTopic: Which creatures and objects a pit owner pays for, the search for the right פסוק, and רבי יוחנן's reading of 'שור חרש שוטה וקטן'
overview: The גמרא keeps reading the פסוק about a בור (שמות 21:33-34) to work out which creatures a pit owner must pay for. First it explains that the רבנן need the word או to teach that one animal alone is enough. רבי יהודה learns this from the singular word ונפל instead. The גמרא then tries a כלל ופרט וכלל to include all living creatures, but that reading could leave out birds, and the attempt to save it fails. Next it tries ״וְהַמֵּת יִהְיֶה לוֹ״ (anything that can die) and defends it on the question of vessels. That source is dropped because רבא needs the same פסוק for a different law. The final source is ״כֶּסֶף יָשִׁיב לִבְעָלָיו״ (anything with an owner), with ״שׁוֹר״ leaving out people and ״חֲמוֹר״ leaving out vessels. רבא admits that for רבי יהודה the word ״חֲמוֹר״ stays unexplained, just like ״שֶׂה״ in אבידה. Finally, רבי יוחנן explains that the משנה's 'חרש, שוטה, וקטן' ox describes the ox itself, not its owner.

steps.title: The word או teaches that each animal counts on its own
steps.stepSummary: The רבנן need the word או to separate the ox and the donkey, so the owner of the pit is liable even when only one of them falls in.
steps.simpleTranslation: The word 'or' is needed to separate the cases.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains what the רבנן learn from the small word או in the פסוק. It tells us that either animal alone is enough to make the owner of the pit liable.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Without או, someone might read 'an ox and a donkey' as one combined case, as if both had to fall in. The word או splits them apart. Because the רבנן use או for this, they cannot use it to include vessels the way רבי יהודה does (step 10 mentions his view).

keyTerms.meaning: to separate, to teach that each item counts by itself
it is needed for (a different teaching)

phrases.english: 'Or' is needed to separate.
phrases.notes: This means an ox alone, or a donkey alone, is enough. Both do not need to fall in together.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the earlier discussion of how each side reads the words of the פסוק.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Assigns the word או a necessary job
steps.terutzMaskana: For the רבנן, או teaches that each animal is a separate case.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The owner of a בור is liable even if only one animal falls in.

steps.title: רבי יהודה learns the separation from the word ונפל
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהודה does not need או for separating, because he learns it from the singular verb ונפל ('and it falls').
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבי יהודה learns 'to separate' from the word 'and it falls'.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains how רבי יהודה knows that one animal alone is enough. He gets it from a different word, so או stays free for him to include vessels.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The verb ונפל is singular: 'it falls'. That suggests even one animal falling in makes the owner liable. So רבי יהודה does not need או for this teaching.

keyTerms.meaning: 'and it falls', a singular verb in the פסוק
it is derived, it comes out from

phrases.english: And Rabbi Yehuda: 'to separate' comes out from 'and it falls'.
phrases.notes: The singular form 'it falls' points to just one animal.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains how רבי יהודה gets the same teaching from a different word.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Where does רבי יהודה learn that each animal counts on its own?

steps.title: The רבנן: ונפל can also mean many
steps.stepSummary: The רבנן do not accept the proof from ונפל, because a singular verb can still describe several animals.
steps.simpleTranslation: And the רבנן hold that 'and it falls' can mean many.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains why the רבנן do not learn separation from ונפל. In their view, the word does not prove that only one animal is meant.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The רבנן say a singular verb in the תורה can still cover many items. So ונפל could still mean an ox and a donkey together. That is why they need או to teach separation.
steps.whatToRemember: Both sides agree that one animal alone is enough. רבי יהודה learns it from ונפל, and the רבנן learn it from או.

phrases.english: And the Rabbis: 'and it falls' implies many.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the רבנן's reason for not using רבי יהודה's source.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects learning separation from ונפל, according to the רבנן.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: A singular verb can still describe many items.

steps.title: Maybe the פסוק is a כלל ופרט, which would limit it to an ox and a donkey
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא suggests that ונפל is a כלל and 'ox and donkey' is a פרט. By the rule of כלל ופרט, only an ox and a donkey would be covered.
steps.simpleTranslation: Say that 'and it falls' is a general statement, and 'ox and donkey' is a detail. With a general statement followed by a detail, the general statement includes only what is in the detail. So an ox and a donkey are covered, and anything else is not.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges both views with a rule of reading the תורה. If the פסוק is a כלל ופרט, the law of בור would apply only to an ox and a donkey.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Under the rule of כלל ופרט, a general word that is followed by specific examples is limited to those examples. That would mean the owner of a pit pays only for an ox or a donkey. It would not cover other animals, even though we assume it does.

keyTerms.meaning: a general statement followed by a detail; only the detail is included

phrases.english: Say: 'and it falls' is a generalization,
'ox and donkey' is a detail;
a generalization and a detail:
the generalization contains only what is in the detail;
ox and donkey, yes,
anything else, no!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Uses the same פסוק to raise a new problem about how far the law reaches.
steps.kashyaTarget: The assumption that the law of בור covers all animals.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Reading the פסוק as a כלל ופרט limits it to an ox and a donkey alone.

steps.title: A second כלל makes it a כלל ופרט וכלל, which covers all living creatures
steps.stepSummary: The next פסוק, 'the owner of the pit shall pay', is a second general statement. A כלל ופרט וכלל includes everything similar to the detail, which here means all living creatures.
steps.simpleTranslation: They answered: 'The owner of the pit shall pay' is a second general statement. With a general statement, a detail, and a general statement, you include only things similar to the detail. Just as the detail lists living creatures, so too all living creatures are included.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge by pointing to the following פסוק. Because a second כלל comes after the פרט, the pattern is כלל ופרט וכלל, and that pattern widens the law.
steps.deeperAnalysis: With a כלל ופרט וכלל, the law reaches anything that resembles the detail. An ox and a donkey are living creatures, so every living creature is covered. Other things, such as objects, would not be included by this reading.

keyTerms.meaning: it went back and made another general statement
general, detail, general; includes whatever is similar to the detail

steps.confusionAlert: Do not mix up the two rules. כלל ופרט limits the law to the detail itself. כלל ופרט וכלל widens it to anything similar to the detail.

phrases.english: They said: 'The owner of the pit shall pay' — it went back and generalized.
A generalization, a detail, and a generalization:

phrases.aramaic: אִי אַתָּה דָן אֶלָּא כְעֵין הַפְּרָט;
phrases.english: you may only include what is similar to the detail;
just as the explicit detail is living creatures,
so too all living creatures.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the כלל ופרט challenge.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Finds a second כלל, which changes which reading rule applies
steps.terutzHavaAmina: A כלל ופרט would cover only an ox and a donkey.
steps.terutzMaskana: A כלל ופרט וכלל covers all living creatures.
steps.whyThisMatters: This is how the גמרא shows that the owner of a pit is liable for any animal that falls in, not only an ox or a donkey.

steps.title: Maybe 'similar to the detail' leaves out birds
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא pushes back: an ox and a donkey are creatures whose נבלה causes טומאה by touch and by carrying. If that is the shared feature, birds would not be covered.
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, maybe it means this: just as the explicit detail is something whose carcass makes a person impure by touch and by carrying, so too everything whose carcass makes a person impure by touch and by carrying is covered. But birds are not.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the answer it just gave. It asks which feature of the ox and the donkey we should copy, and suggests one that would leave birds out.
steps.deeperAnalysis: With a כלל ופרט וכלל, everything depends on what 'similar' means. An ox and a donkey share a narrower feature as well: their נבלה causes טומאה through touch and carrying. If we use that feature, birds fall outside the law of בור.

keyTerms.meaning: the carcass of an animal that died without proper שחיטה

phrases.english: If so, just as the explicit detail
is something whose carcass makes impure by touch and by carrying,
so too everything whose carcass
makes impure by touch and by carrying,
but birds, no!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer in step 5 by suggesting a narrower shared feature.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that 'similar to the detail' means all living creatures.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ox and the donkey also share a narrower feature, that their נבלה causes טומאה by touch and carrying, and that feature would exclude birds.

steps.title: If that were the point, one example would be enough
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers the challenge from step 6. If the shared feature were only 'its carcass causes טומאה', the תורה would have written just one example, not two.
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, the Torah should have written only one detail!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is defending the כלל ופרט וכלל reading. It argues that the תורה would not need both 'ox' and 'donkey' just to teach 'animals whose carcass causes טומאה'.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both an ox and a donkey share the feature of causing טומאה by touching and carrying. One of them alone would have been enough to teach that feature. Writing two examples must mean the category is wider, wide enough to include birds.

keyTerms.meaning: 'The Merciful One', a name for ה׳ as the Giver of the Torah
A detail or specific example in a פסוק
'If so', which introduces what would follow from the other side's idea

phrases.english: If so,
let the Merciful One write just one detail!

steps.triggerLanguage: אִם כֵּן, נִכְתּוֹב רַחֲמָנָא חַד פְּרָטָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 6 by arguing that two examples point to a broader category.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Argument from extra wording: two examples where one would do
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The shared feature of ox and donkey is טומאה by touch and carrying, so birds are left out.
steps.terutzMaskana: Since the Torah gave two examples, the category must be broader than that one feature.

steps.title: Both ox and donkey are really needed
steps.stepSummary: The defense fails. Each animal teaches something the other could not, so both had to be written. The problem from step 6 comes back.
steps.simpleTranslation: Which one should it write? If it wrote 'ox', I would say: something brought on the מזבח, yes; something not brought on the מזבח, no. And if the Torah wrote 'donkey', I would say: an animal whose firstborn is holy, yes; one whose firstborn is not holy, no!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא shows that writing only one example would have misled us. That is why the תורה needed both. This knocks down the answer in step 7.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each example has its own special feature. An ox can be brought on the מזבח, and a donkey has בכורה holiness. With only one of them, we would limit the law to that feature, so the second example is not extra. This means step 7's proof from the 'extra' example fails, and the challenge of step 6 (birds would be left out) is back.

keyTerms.meaning: Its firstborn has holiness (like a firstborn donkey, which must be redeemed)
'I would have said', a mistaken idea we might have had

steps.confusionAlert: This step is not explaining why birds are included. It shows that step 7's answer does not work, which is why the גמרא then says אֶלָּא and starts over.

phrases.english: Which one should it write?
If it wrote 'ox', I would have said:
something offered on the altar, yes,
something not offered on the altar, no.
And if the Merciful One wrote 'donkey', I would have said:
one whose firstborn is holy, yes,
one whose firstborn is not holy, no!

steps.triggerLanguage: הֵי נִכְתּוֹב? אִי כְּתַב ״שׁוֹר״, הֲוָה אָמֵינָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges step 7 by showing that both examples are needed.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The claim in step 7 that one example would have been enough.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: Each example alone would wrongly narrow the law to its own special feature (מזבח or בכורה), so both are needed.

steps.title: A new source: anything that can die
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא drops the כלל ופרט וכלל approach. It learns instead from ״וְהַמֵּת יִהְיֶה לוֹ״ that the owner of a בור pays for any creature that can die, birds included.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, the פסוק says: 'And the dead one shall be his', which includes anything that can die.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives up the old method and brings a new פסוק as the source for including all living creatures.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word 'dead' in the פסוק sets the category as anything that is able to die. That includes birds and all creatures, so the problem from step 6 is gone.

keyTerms.meaning: 'Rather', which drops the earlier approach and starts a new one

steps.whyThisMatters: The next several steps test this source. It survives the questions about vessels (steps 10-13), but in step 14 it is set aside, because the verse is needed for רבא's teaching.

phrases.english: Rather, the verse says:
'And the dead one shall be his'
anything that is subject to death.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Replaces the כלל ופרט וכלל source, which failed in step 8.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Inclusion comes from כלל ופרט וכלל, which leaves out birds.
steps.terutzMaskana: Inclusion comes from ״וְהַמֵּת״: anything that can die.

steps.title: Can vessels die?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the new source. Both the רבנן and רבי יהודה treat vessels in a בור as something a פסוק must teach about. But vessels cannot die!
steps.simpleTranslation: Both for the רבנן, who exclude vessels, and for רבי יהודה, who includes vessels, are vessels things that can die?!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the new source from step 9. If a בור only covers things that can die, why do both opinions discuss vessels at all?
steps.deeperAnalysis: The רבנן need a פסוק to leave vessels out, and רבי יהודה uses a פסוק to bring them in. Both act as if vessels could have been part of the law of בור. But if the rule is 'only things that can die', vessels would be outside it from the start.

keyTerms.meaning: 'Are they?', often used in a challenging question

phrases.aramaic: בֵּין לְרַבָּנַן דְּקָא מְמַעֲטִי לְהוּ לְכֵלִים,
phrases.english: Both according to the Rabbis, who exclude vessels,

phrases.aramaic: וּבֵין לְרַבִּי יְהוּדָה דְּקָא מְרַבֵּי לְהוּ לְכֵלִים –
phrases.english: and according to Rabbi Yehuda, who includes vessels,
are vessels subject to death?!

steps.triggerLanguage: בֵּין לְרַבָּנַן דְּקָא מְמַעֲטִי לְהוּ לְכֵלִים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the new source from step 9.
steps.kashyaTarget: The source ״וְהַמֵּת״ = anything that can die.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Vessels cannot die, yet both opinions treat vessels as a question for בור, which suggests 'death' is not the defining category.

steps.title: Breaking is a vessel's death
steps.stepSummary: The answer: for a vessel, being broken counts as its 'death'.
steps.simpleTranslation: They said: their breaking is their death.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge of step 10 by widening what 'death' means for objects.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A vessel that breaks is 'dead', because it stops working as a vessel. So vessels can fit the category of 'things that can die', and the debate about them makes sense.

phrases.english: They said:
their breaking is their death.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 10.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Death applies only to living things.
steps.terutzMaskana: For vessels, breaking counts as death.

steps.title: According to רב, can bad air harm vessels?
steps.stepSummary: A new challenge using רב's view: a בור is only liable for damage from its bad air, not from the blow of the fall. Bad air cannot hurt vessels, so why discuss them?
steps.simpleTranslation: And according to רב, who said: the בור the Torah made one liable for is for its bad air, not for the blow of the fall. Both for the רבנן and for רבי יהודה, are vessels affected by bad air?!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a second attack. Even if breaking counts as death, רב says a בור only damages through its bad air, and that seems not to affect vessels.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The answer in step 11 works if a fall can break a vessel. But רב holds that the תורה made a בור liable only for its bad air. Air does not break pots, so vessels again seem to fall outside the law of בור.

keyTerms.meaning: Bad air or fumes in a pit
The blow or impact of the fall

phrases.english: And according to Rav, who said:
the pit for which the Torah made one liable
is for its bad air and not for its impact;
phrases.notes: Bad air at the bottom of the pit is what kills, not the hit from falling in.

phrases.english: both according to the Rabbis and according to Rabbi Yehuda,
are vessels affected by bad air?!

steps.triggerLanguage: וּלְרַב דְּאָמַר: בּוֹר שֶׁחִיְּיבָה עָלָיו תּוֹרָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second challenge, using רב's view of how a בור damages.
steps.kashyaTarget: The idea that vessels can belong to the law of בור.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If a בור only damages through bad air, vessels could never be damaged by it, so neither opinion should need to discuss them.

steps.title: New vessels crack from bad air
steps.stepSummary: The answer: new vessels can crack from the bad air of a pit, so vessels can be harmed in a way that fits רב's view.
steps.simpleTranslation: They said: this is about new vessels, which crack from bad air.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers step 12 with a real case where bad air does damage vessels.
steps.deeperAnalysis: New vessels are delicate enough to crack from the fumes. So even according to רב, vessels can be damaged by a בור. That means the debate between the רבנן and רבי יהודה still makes sense.
steps.whatToRemember: So far, the source ״וְהַמֵּת יִהְיֶה לוֹ״ (anything that can 'die') holds up on the question of vessels. For vessels, 'death' means breaking, and even by רב's bad-air view, new vessels can crack from the fumes. The next step attacks this source from a different angle.

phrases.english: They said: with new ones,
which crack from the bad air.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 12.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Bad air cannot harm vessels at all.
steps.terutzMaskana: New vessels crack from bad air, so vessels can be damaged by a בור even according to רב.

steps.title: The verse about the carcass is already used by רבא
steps.stepSummary: The source ״וְהַמֵּת יִהְיֶה לוֹ״ is challenged, because רבא already uses it to exempt a pit owner when a פסולי המוקדשין ox falls in.
steps.simpleTranslation: But this verse, "and the carcass shall be his," is needed for רבא's teaching. רבא said: if a disqualified consecrated ox fell into a pit, the pit owner is exempt. The verse says "the carcass shall be his," so it speaks about an owner whose carcass belongs to him. That leaves out this owner, whose carcass does not belong to him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the source from step 9. That פסוק is already busy teaching a different law, so it cannot also be the source for birds.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבא reads ״וְהַמֵּת יִהְיֶה לוֹ״ as a limit: the pit owner pays only when the dead animal's body belongs to its owner. Since the פסוק is already used up for that rule, the גמרא assumes it cannot also teach that every creature that can die is included.

keyTerms.meaning: Animals that were set aside as קרבנות but became disqualified, usually through a blemish
It is needed for (this פסוק is already used for another teaching)
"And the carcass shall be his" (the pit owner gives up the dead animal to its owner)
Excluding; this case is left out

phrases.english: This verse, "and the carcass shall be his"
is needed for רבא's teaching,
as רבא said:
A disqualified consecrated ox
that fell into a pit: the pit owner is exempt,
as it says: "and the carcass shall be his"
meaning an owner whose carcass belongs to him,
which leaves out this one, whose carcass does not belong to him.

steps.triggerLanguage: הַאי ״וְהַמֵּת יִהְיֶה לוֹ״ מִבְּעֵי לֵיהּ לְכִדְרָבָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Goes back to attack the source from step 9, after steps 10-13 had defended it on the issue of vessels.
steps.kashyaTarget: Using ״וְהַמֵּת יִהְיֶה לוֹ״ as the source that every creature that can die is included in בור
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A פסוק already used for רבא's exemption (פסולי המוקדשין) cannot also serve as the source for a second teaching.

steps.title: A new source: "money he shall return to its owner"
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא switches to ״כֶּסֶף יָשִׁיב לִבְעָלָיו״, which includes anything that has an owner.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, the verse says: "money he shall return to its owner." This comes to include anything that has an owner.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives up on the carcass verse and finds a different פסוק to include birds and all other animals.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word ״לִבְעָלָיו״ (to its owner) is read broadly. Anything that has an owner is included in the pit owner's duty to pay, so birds are covered without needing ״וְהַמֵּת יִהְיֶה לוֹ״.

keyTerms.meaning: "Money he shall return to its owner" (the pit owner pays)

phrases.english: Rather, the verse says:
"Money he shall return to its owner"
to include anything that has an owner.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 14 by replacing the source that was used up.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The inclusion of all creatures came from ״וְהַמֵּת יִהְיֶה לוֹ״.
steps.terutzMaskana: The inclusion comes from ״כֶּסֶף יָשִׁיב לִבְעָלָיו״: anything with an owner.

steps.title: Then people and vessels should be included too
steps.stepSummary: If anything with an owner is included, then vessels and even people should be included, which no one holds for people.
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, even vessels and a person should be included too!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on the new source. It seems to include too much.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Vessels have owners, and a slave also has an owner. But the pit owner does not pay for a person according to anyone, and the רבנן say he does not pay for vessels. So "anything with an owner" is too broad.

phrases.english: If so,
even vessels and a person should be included too!

steps.triggerLanguage: אִי הָכִי, אֲפִילּוּ כֵּלִים וְאָדָם נָמֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the new source from step 15.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If ownership is the only test, people and vessels would be included, which goes against the accepted law.

steps.title: "Ox" leaves out people, "donkey" leaves out vessels
steps.stepSummary: The words ״שׁוֹר״ and ״חֲמוֹר״ in the פסוק limit the inclusion: no people and no vessels.
steps.simpleTranslation: The verse says "ox," and not a person; "donkey," and not vessels.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the פסוק itself narrows the broad inclusion by naming an ox and a donkey.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each named animal has a job. ״שׁוֹר״ teaches that the pit owner does not pay for a person, and ״חֲמוֹר״ teaches that he does not pay for vessels. Everything else with an owner, like birds, stays included.

keyTerms.meaning: Ox; here used to leave out a person
Donkey; here used to leave out vessels
And not; this case is left out

phrases.english: The verse says "ox," and not a person,
"donkey," and not vessels.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 16 by showing how the פסוק excludes people and vessels.
steps.terutzMaskana: ״שׁוֹר״ leaves out people and ״חֲמוֹר״ leaves out vessels; everything else with an owner is included.

steps.title: For רבי יהודה, what does "donkey" leave out?
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהודה holds the pit owner pays for vessels, so for him the word ״חֲמוֹר״ cannot be leaving out vessels.
steps.simpleTranslation: But according to רבי יהודה, who includes vessels: it makes sense that "ox" leaves out a person. But "donkey," what does he leave out with it?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the answer of step 17 from the view of רבי יהודה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 17 needs ״חֲמוֹר״ to leave out vessels. But רבי יהודה includes vessels in בור, so for him ״חֲמוֹר״ has nothing to leave out. The word seems to have no job.

keyTerms.meaning: It makes sense that (agreeing to one part before asking about another)

phrases.english: And according to רבי יהודה
who includes vessels,
it makes sense that with "ox" he leaves out a person,
but "donkey," what does he leave out with it?

steps.triggerLanguage: וּלְרַבִּי יְהוּדָה דְּקָא מְרַבֵּי לְהוּ לְכֵלִים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges step 17 using רבי יהודה's view that vessels are included (mentioned in step 10).
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that ״חֲמוֹר״ leaves out vessels
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: For רבי יהודה vessels are included, so ״חֲמוֹר״ is left with no job.

steps.title: רבא admits two words stay unexplained
steps.stepSummary: רבא concludes that ״חֲמוֹר״ in בור (for רבי יהודה) and ״שֶׂה״ in אבידה (for everyone) remain a קשיא.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, רבא said: the word "donkey" in the laws of a pit, according to רבי יהודה, and the word "sheep" in the laws of a lost object, according to everyone, are difficult.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא does not answer the question. He admits the word ״חֲמוֹר״ is unexplained for רבי יהודה, and adds another word with the same problem.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Instead of forcing an answer, רבא points to a similar case. In the laws of returning lost objects, the word ״שֶׂה״ also seems to teach nothing, according to everyone. Both words are left as an open קשיא, but the source ״כֶּסֶף יָשִׁיב לִבְעָלָיו״ is not rejected.

keyTerms.meaning: A difficulty that stays without an answer
A lost object that must be returned

steps.whatToRemember: The source that a pit owner pays for anything with an owner is ״כֶּסֶף יָשִׁיב לִבְעָלָיו״. ״שׁוֹר״ leaves out people. According to the רבנן, ״חֲמוֹר״ leaves out vessels. For רבי יהודה, who includes vessels, ״חֲמוֹר״ stays unexplained, just like ״שֶׂה״ in אבידה.
steps.confusionAlert: Here קַשְׁיָא does not mean the whole approach falls. It means these specific words remain unexplained, while the main source stays in place.

phrases.english: Rather, רבא said:
"Donkey" in the laws of a pit, according to רבי יהודה,
and "sheep" in the laws of a lost object, according to everyone,
are difficult.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא אָמַר רָבָא: ״חֲמוֹר״ דְּבוֹר לְרַבִּי יְהוּדָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Responds to step 18 by admitting the difficulty instead of resolving it.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: ״חֲמוֹר״ in בור for רבי יהודה and ״שֶׂה״ in אבידה for everyone have no clear teaching; this stays a קשיא.

steps.title: The משנה: a deaf, unsound, or young ox falls into the pit
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה's ruling that the pit owner is חייב if a חרש, שוטה, or קטן ox fell into his pit.
steps.simpleTranslation: If a deaf, mentally unsound, or young ox fell into the pit, the pit owner is liable.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes a new line from the משנה so it can examine it. This sets up the question that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ruling itself is clear: the pit owner pays. What is unclear is the phrase "שׁוֹר חֵרֵשׁ שׁוֹטֶה וְקָטָן". It could describe the ox's owner or the ox itself.
steps.confusionAlert: Normally חרש, שוטה, and קטן describe people: a deaf-mute, a mentally unsound person, and a minor. The whole question here is whether they describe people or the ox itself.

phrases.english: If an ox fell into it
phrases.notes: "It" is the pit (בור) that the משנה has been talking about.

phrases.english: deaf, unsound, or young, he is liable.

steps.triggerLanguage: נָפַל לְתוֹכוֹ שׁוֹר חֵרֵשׁ שׁוֹטֶה וְקָטָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves on from the discussion of ״חֲמוֹר״ and ״שֶׂה״ to the next line of the משנה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The pit owner is חייב when a חרש, שוטה, or קטן ox falls into his pit.

steps.title: What does the phrase mean?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what the משנה means by a חרש, שוטה, or קטן ox.
steps.simpleTranslation: What does "a deaf, unsound, or young ox" mean?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks for the meaning of the words in the משנה. This opens the discussion that follows.
steps.deeperAnalysis: These words usually describe people, so it is unclear how they apply to an ox. The גמרא wants to know who or what is being described.

phrases.english: What is "a deaf, unsound, or young ox"?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions the wording of the משנה just quoted.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether the words חרש, שוטה, and קטן describe the ox's owner or the ox itself.

steps.title: It cannot mean the ox's owner
steps.stepSummary: If the phrase meant an ox owned by a חרש, שוטה, or קטן, then a healthy adult's ox would be פטור, which is impossible.
steps.simpleTranslation: If you say it means an ox belonging to a deaf-mute, an unsound person, or a minor, then an ox belonging to a competent adult would be exempt?!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tries the first reading, that the words describe the owner, and shows that it leads to a ridiculous result.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the משנה made the pit owner pay specifically for an ox owned by these people, that would suggest he does not pay for a normal adult's ox. Nobody would say that, so this reading is rejected.

keyTerms.meaning: If you say (introduces a reading that will be rejected)

phrases.english: If you say an ox of a deaf-mute,

phrases.aramaic: שׁוֹר שֶׁל שׁוֹטֶה, שׁוֹר שֶׁל קָטָן –
phrases.english: an ox of an unsound person, an ox of a minor,
then an ox of a competent adult would be exempt?!
phrases.notes: This is said with surprise: obviously the pit owner pays for a normal adult's ox too.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Tests a possible answer to the question and shows that it fails.
steps.kashyaTarget: The reading that the words describe the ox's owner.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Inference from the opposite case: naming these owners implies that a פקח's ox is פטור, which is absurd.

steps.title: רבי יוחנן: the words describe the ox itself
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן explains that the משנה means an ox that is itself deaf, mentally unsound, or young.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוחנן says: an ox that is deaf, an ox that is unsound, an ox that is young.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יוחנן gives the correct reading of the משנה: the descriptions belong to the ox, not to its owner.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Once the words describe the ox's condition, the strange inference about a פקח's ox disappears. The משנה is now teaching that the pit owner is חייב even for an ox that is deaf, unsound, or very young.
steps.whatToRemember: In this משנה, "חרש, שוטה, וקטן" describe the ox's own condition, not its owner. This is רבי יוחנן's reading.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yochanan said:

phrases.aramaic: שׁוֹר שֶׁהוּא חֵרֵשׁ, שׁוֹר שֶׁהוּא שׁוֹטֶה,
phrases.english: An ox that is deaf, an ox that is unsound,
an ox that is young.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן: שׁוֹר שֶׁהוּא חֵרֵשׁ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question by giving a new reading that avoids the problem raised.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The words describe the ox's owner, which would mean a פקח's ox is פטור.
steps.terutzMaskana: The words describe the ox itself: deaf, unsound, or young, and the pit owner is חייב.
